summary: Describes how IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are bound to MPEG-2 Transport Streams, called address resolution, complementing higher-layer discovery tools. An IP address must be associated with a PID value and a specific transmission network. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Digital TV broadcasts carry data on numbered channels. This note explains how to match internet addresses to those channels.

questions: how to resolve ip addresses over mpeg-2
what is address resolution for mpeg-2 networks
how does ip work over mpeg-2
how do broadcast networks resolve ip addresses
why is multicast important for mpeg-2
subtitle: How to find IP addresses in digital TV broadcast transmission streams.

tldr.problem: Digital TV broadcasts (DVB, ATSC) use MPEG-2 streams to send audio, video, and data. When IP datagrams are encapsulated in these streams, receivers need to find which numbered channel (PID) carries a specific IP address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes multiple methods: static configuration, MPEG-2 signaling tables (INT, AIT, MMT), IP protocols (DHCP, ARP, Neighbor Discovery), and link-layer mechanisms that allow receivers to map IP addresses to the correct transmission channel.
tldr.outcome: Networks using IP over MPEG-2 (satellite, cable, terrestrial TV) can efficiently deliver IP services by advertising address bindings through the broadcast channel itself, reducing the need for external configuration.

today: RFC 4947 is Informational and remains a reference for deploying IP services over MPEG-2 broadcast networks. It is particularly relevant for DVB, ATSC, and DOCSIS networks using satellite, cable, or terrestrial transmission.

sections.title: IP Over Digital TV Broadcasts
sections.content:
MPEG-2 is the standard used by digital TV systems (DVB in Europe, ATSC in the Americas, and others) to encode audio, video, and data for broadcast. An MPEG-2 Transport Stream is a sequence of fixed 188-byte packets, each labeled with a 13-bit Packet ID (PID) that identifies which logical channel it belongs to.

Receivers watching the broadcast tune to a Transmission Multiplex (a bundle of channels sent together) and filter packets by PID, extracting just the content they want. IP datagrams can be encapsulated in these packets, allowing the broadcast to deliver internet data directly to receivers.

The challenge: when a receiver wants to receive an IP multicast group (e.g., a live sports stream) or reach a unicast service (e.g., an internet server), it must first know which PID carries the IP traffic. This binding of IP address to PID is called Address Resolution.
sections.eli5: A digital broadcast sends many channels (numbered 1, 2, 3, etc.). Some carry movies, some carry sports, some carry the internet. You need to know: which channel number has the content you want?

sections.title: What Needs to Be Resolved
sections.content:
Address resolution in MPEG-2 networks has two parts: MPEG-2-level resolution and IP-level resolution.

At the MPEG-2 level, a receiver must associate an IP address (or IP multicast group) with a specific PID value on a specific Transmission Multiplex. This is the lower-layer problem.

At the IP level, a receiver must associate an IP address with a Network Point of Attachment (NPA) address (similar to an Ethernet MAC address). This is needed for link-layer forwarding and routing decisions.

Receivers may face address scope issues: MPEG-2 networks can carry multiple independent IP networks, and packets must not leak from one scope to another. For example, private IPv4 addresses (10/8, 192.168/16) or link-local addresses must be confined to the correct network.

For multicast, the challenge is greater: a single IP multicast group might be available on multiple PIDs or even multiple transmission multiplexes (Simulcasting). Receivers must avoid receiving duplicates while ensuring the group is accessible.
sections.eli5: A receiver needs to know three things: (1) which channel (PID) has my internet address, (2) which broadcast (transmission multiplex) to tune to, and (3) what is the MAC-like address for my receiving interface. Also, for live TV groups, avoid watching the same show twice on two channels.

sections.title: Methods of Address Resolution
sections.content:
The RFC describes four main approaches:

Static Configuration: The PID-to-IP mappings are pre-configured manually or at installation time. This works for closed, controlled networks (cable modems, corporate broadcast) where the set of addresses is known in advance. DOCSIS cable networks use this: all downstream IP traffic goes to a single well-known PID, and DHCP is used to configure IP addresses.

MPEG-2 Table-Based Resolution: Signaling tables are broadcast in the MPEG-2 stream itself. The IP/MAC Notification Table (INT) from the DVB standard associates IPv4/IPv6 addresses and MAC addresses with PIDs and multiplexes. The Multicast Mapping Table (MMT) and Application Information Table (AIT) are proprietary extensions used by some broadcast systems. Receivers parse these tables periodically (updating is infrequent) to learn address bindings.

IP-Based Address Resolution: Standard IP protocols handle the resolution. DHCP assigns IP addresses to receivers. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery resolve IP addresses to MAC/NPA addresses at Layer 2. For multicast, the receiver can use IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) or IPv6 MLD to announce group membership, signaling to the network which multicast groups it wants to receive.

IP-Based PID Selection: Some systems use a hash or mapping function to distribute IP multicast addresses across multiple PIDs (similar to how Ethernet maps IP multicast to MAC addresses). This avoids the need for explicit PID-per-address registration.
sections.eli5: You can tell the receiver beforehand which channels to watch. Or the broadcast itself tells you (in special control messages). Or the receiver asks the network using standard internet protocols like DHCP and Neighbor Discovery.

sections.title: Unicast vs. Multicast Challenges
sections.content:
Unicast: A receiver needs to learn the PID of a unicast service (e.g., a live camera feed sent to only one subscriber). For unidirectional broadcast links (satellite downlink only), the receiver cannot query; instead, it relies on static configuration or MPEG-2 table broadcasts. For bidirectional links (some cable or terrestrial networks), the receiver can use DHCP or other IP protocols to request an address and learn the associated PID from an AR Server.

Multicast: IP multicast is a natural fit for broadcast networks since MPEG-2 natively supports sending the same content to many receivers. However, challenges include:

  • Large group sets: A broadcast network may peered to the multicast-enabled Internet may need to support thousands of active multicast groups, each with a unique PID. Sending detailed tables for every group is impractical.
  • Dynamic membership: Groups form and dissolve dynamically. The broadcast stream cannot update tables fast enough for ephemeral groups.
  • Hash-based distribution: Some systems use a deterministic hash function to map IP multicast addresses to PIDs. This avoids explicit signaling but requires all receivers to use the same hash formula.
  • Simulcast duplication: When the same multicast content is available on multiple PIDs (for load balancing or redundancy), receivers must suppress duplicates or select a single source.
sections.eli5: For a live interview sent to one person: tell them the channel number in advance. For a live sports broadcast sent to everyone interested: the network announces which channels carry different sports, but popular events may appear on multiple channels to share the load.

sections.title: Bridging, Routing, and Link-Layer Details
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes between routed networks and bridged networks. In a routed setup, an Encapsulator (the broadcast source) sends IP datagrams directly. In a bridged setup, IP frames are encapsulated with Ethernet-like headers; Bridges learn the MAC/NPA addresses of downstream receivers and forward accordingly.

Two MPEG-2 encapsulation methods are discussed: Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE) [RFC4326] and Multiprotocol Encapsulation (MPE). Both support carrying IP datagrams, with options for including a destination MAC/NPA address to support bridging.

For unidirectional links with no return channel (e.g., satellite downlink), address resolution must work with one-way traffic only. The broadcast itself advertises what services are available. Unicast replies use a separate return link (e.g., satellite uplink or terrestrial return channel).

For bidirectional links, standard IP protocols (ARP, DHCP, IPv6 ND) can be used, reducing complexity. The AR Server can be a dedicated device or integrated into the Encapsulator.
sections.eli5: A bridge passes data between two networks; a router looks up the address and chooses where to send it. On a broadcast link, bridges need to know which receiver MAC address to send unicast to. One-way broadcast (satellite downlink only) is trickier than two-way links.
